before_faq: No single architect. Donato Bramante drew the first plan in 1506 (a domed, centrally planned design); Raphael and his collaborators changed it to a Latin cross after Bramante's 1514 death; the architect Pope Paul III put in charge after restarting the project in 1534 undid that shift and returned the design to Bramante's earlier circular layout; Michelangelo, chief architect from 1546 until his death in 1564, carried the dome as far as its base ring before he died; della Porta finished it with Fontana's help in 1588–90, revising the plan Michelangelo left behind; and Carlo Maderno reversed the plan a second time from 1607 onward, extending it into the Latin-cross nave visitors walk through now. Bernini later added the baldachin and the piazza colonnade. (Source: Britannica's entries on the basilica and on Carlo Maderno; the Vatican's basilica office.)

A century and two decades separate the foundation ceremony from the dedication. The first ceremony, presided over by Julius II, took place on 18 April 1506. The second followed under Urban VIII on 18 November 1626. The dedication's fourth centenary therefore falls on 18 November 2026. The chronology comes from the basilica's custodians; reports published in April 2026 describe the anniversary programme.

About 187 meters long for the main structure. The basilica's own official public FAQ page states that figure directly, and Britannica arrives at the same number measuring in feet. before_faq: Kahlo left the hair between her eyebrows in place. The V&A quotes her writing, \"Of my face, I like the eyebrows and the eyes.\" She also darkened her brows with cosmetics. A Revlon eyebrow pencil in Ebony was found among her possessions in 2004. Her self-portraits repeat the connected brow shape. [The V&A account of her cosmetics](https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/making-her-self-up) describes how she kept and enhanced her eyebrows.

Estimates cluster around 150 total paintings. Taschen published a catalogue of her complete paintings in 2021 with Luis-Martín Lozano as editor. The publisher itself describes it as gathering \"all 152\" of her paintings. That figure builds on a 1988 raisonné catalogue that scholar Prignitz-Poda co-authored with two colleagues. The Ransom Center reports that self-portraits account for 55 of the total.

Neither, conclusively. Twelve Kahlo scholars and the trust controlling her copyright declared the Noyolas' archive fraudulent and asked Mexico's government to look into its origins. Owner Carlos Noyola countered with his own hired expert's handwriting comparison plus a paint-dating test that matched the 1940s. No public government ruling has settled the dispute since it broke in 2009.

It disappeared after being exhibited in Warsaw in 1955 and has never been recovered. A 2019 attempted sale in Morelos state, Mexico, and a 2020 claim by a Spanish dealer to have located it in a warehouse in London were both rejected by authorities and experts. Prignitz-Poda noted that the 2020 painting was on canvas, unlike the genuine wood panel.

Yes. Bavarian authorities confirmed on October 27, 2025, that they had seized a batch of counterfeit paintings, with false attributions covering Kahlo, Rembrandt, Miró, Modigliani, and Picasso. The raids spanned Germany, Switzerland, and Liechtenstein, targeting a 77-year-old main suspect along with ten accomplices. Investigations were ongoing at the time of the announcement.

The Two Fridas hangs in Mexico City's museum of modern art; Mexico's INBA acquired it in 1947, then moved it to its current home by 1966. Her other self-portrait, the 1940 piece involving a hummingbird and thorn necklace, is held in Texas by the Ransom Center, part of the Nickolas Muray collection acquired in 1965.

Because the catalogue is small and mostly closed, roughly 150 paintings against the thousands left by more prolific painters, any claimed new or rediscovered work carries disproportionate weight and value. A 2010 Newsweek report cited a case where an obscure, minor Kahlo landscape fetched ten times its pre-sale estimate at Christie's, evidence that scarcity itself commands a premium in this market and keeps forgery and disputed reattribution attempts worthwhile.

The Two Fridas (1939), now in Mexico City's museum of modern art, is usually named as her single most famous painting; it shows two versions of Kahlo, one in traditional Tehuana dress and one in a European-style gown, painted after her divorce from Diego Rivera. Her other widely reproduced 1940 self-portrait, involving a hummingbird and thorn necklace, is held in Texas by the Ransom Center and appears on more posters, book covers, and prints than any other Kahlo painting.

before_faq: The version now standard in American art classrooms lists seven terms: color, form, line, shape, space, texture, and value. Wikipedia describes them as the stylistic building blocks an artist uses to communicate, and notes that a handful of departments teach two extra categories, the physical trace of an artist's hand and the substance a work is made from, so even the tally is not fully settled.

No single person did. The oldest known formal version traces to a book Arthur Wesley Dow published in 1899, which reduced picture-making to a trio: color, notan, and line. Denman Ross at Harvard and Wassily Kandinsky at the Bauhaus each built parallel systems over the following three decades, and today's classroom checklist of seven terms first turns up in a college textbook, documented in a 1968 printing.

Notan is a Japanese term meaning dark and light. Dow, who introduced the word to American art teaching in his 1899 book Composition, used it to describe how much light a surface bounces back to the eye, in effect how light and dark tones group together across a composition. Today's lists trace their term value straight back to it.

No. His 1926 Bauhaus-era treatise formalized a different, three-part system built from a point, a line, and a plane, treated almost as a branch of geometry. It predates the now-standard seven-term American classroom list and isn't its direct source, though both belong to the same broader history of artists and teachers trying to reduce painting to countable, describable parts.

No. Dow's original 1899 list counted just three. Denman Ross's 1907 book on design theory treated dots, lines, and patches of tone as the working vocabulary, never settling on a fixed count at all. Wikipedia's current entry lists seven core elements and tacks on two more categories that some departments also cover. The number has changed more than once across the documented history of the idea.

Because it works as a shared descriptive vocabulary, not because it's ancient. One major California museum's teaching materials on formal analysis use the same basic terms to help viewers unpack why a picture works the way it does, rather than just naming what's in it, which was the practical problem Arthur Wesley Dow was trying to solve back in 1899 when he first wrote his three-part system down.

A sphere, cube or pyramid is a geometric form: each extends into three dimensions. Sculptures can also have irregular forms resembling living things. The National Gallery of Art uses Alexander Calder's Vertical Constellation with Bomb to teach both kinds. [National Gallery of Art](https://www.nga.gov/educational-resources/elements-art/elements-art-form).

before_faq: In Sanskrit it means circle. The Rig Veda uses that name for its ten textual divisions, a textual arrangement distinct from a drawing; those hymns are conventionally placed around 1500–1200 BCE. A recitation grouping in India's government Vedic catalogue is called Mandala Krama. The age assigned to the hymns does not, by itself, establish when that book label was first used.

No. Drawings occur in manuscripts from Dunhuang made between the eighth and tenth centuries. Japan's Takao mandalas are assigned to AD 824, while surviving Tibetan painted cloths and murals include examples from the 1000s and 1100s. They serve ritual practice in Buddhism, within a Tantric tradition taking shape in India around the 500s CE. Calling the Rig Veda's sections mandalas does not prove that such pictures accompanied the early hymns.

Yes, when made as part of the traditional ritual. Monks build them from colored sand across a multi-day process, consecrate the finished design, then sweep the grains together and release them into a river or stream, a physical reminder that nothing built lasts forever. The Smithsonian staged this itself at its Sackler Gallery, releasing the finished sand into the Tidal Basin in Washington on 27 January 2002. The Dalai Lama carried out that same dismantling ritual during a Kalachakra rite in Leh, Ladakh, on 16 July 2014, ending with the sand poured into the Indus River.

A documented exhibit on Jung's Red Book states that he had already begun sketching circular, mandala-like forms ahead of any study of the Tibetan Buddhist practice behind them, during the years of intense psychological exploration triggered by his split from Sigmund Freud in 1913. He later summarized the circle split into four quarters as a symbol of psychological wholeness, a recurring pattern he believed appeared across unrelated cultures independent of any single religious source, and in 1950 he carved a stone monument at his retreat in Bollingen featuring Telesphorus, an obscure Greek deity linked to healing, worked into a mandala design.

The Met holds several examples, including a late-fourteenth-century cloth painting of the six-armed Jnanadakini, probably made for a Vajravali set of forty-two mandalas. Its exhibition of Tibetan Buddhist mandalas ran from 19 September 2024 to 12 January 2025, with more than 100 objects, chiefly from the eleventh through fifteenth centuries.

before_faq: Cloisonné is a technique for decorating metal objects with colored glass enamel, held in place by thin metal wires bent into a design and soldered or pasted onto the object's surface. The Met describes the process in its essay on the Chinese tradition: the enclosures, called cloisons, are filled with enamel colored by metallic oxide, the piece is fired at roughly 800°C, and because the enamel shrinks after firing, the filling and firing steps are repeated several times before the surface is polished smooth and the exposed wire edges gilded.

Among securely attributed pieces, the Byzantine gold-and-cloisonné reliquary shown at the top of this page ranks among the earliest well-documented examples, probably made in Constantinople and dated to the early 800s CE (broadly around 800 by the Met, narrowed to 843 by other scholarship). Cloisonné-like enameling techniques go back further still, into ancient Mycenaean and Egyptian goldwork, but the fully developed wire-cell technique associated with the word today is best documented starting within Byzantine workshops of the early medieval period.

In cloisonné, the enamel-holding cells, or cloisons, are built up by soldering or pasting metal wire onto the object's surface. In champlevé, the cells are carved, etched, or cast directly into the metal itself, per Wikipedia's explanation of the two methods. Champlevé's cells can be cut into cheaper copper or bronze, while cloisonné traditionally required wire made of gold or silver, a cost difference that helped champlevé spread faster across medieval Western Europe.

Cost was the deciding factor. According to Wikipedia's page on champlevé, its copper and bronze bases were easy to shape and cheap to source, compared with cloisonné's construction from precious-metal wire. Limoges, in France, grew into the largest champlevé production hub by the 1150s, exporting reliquary caskets across Europe at a scale the same entry describes as approaching industrial production. Byzantium itself kept producing cloisonné through this period; the shift away from it was a Western European, cost-driven trend rather than the technique disappearing everywhere.

Kaji Tsunekichi is generally credited with reviving Japan's sculptural cloisonné craft in the late 1830s; he had given up his status as a samurai to work as a metal-gilder in the Owari region. According to Sotheby's, drawing on a profile of Kaji that The Studio published in June 1911, the breakthrough came in roughly 1838, when Kaji dismantled an imported Chinese enamel object to understand its construction. Other, looser popular accounts put the year at 1833 and identify the earlier piece as Dutch instead of Chinese, so the exact year and the piece's origin aren't fully settled between accounts.
after_faq: Cloisonné is a technique for decorating metal objects with colored glass enamel, held in place by thin metal wires bent into a design and soldered or pasted onto the object's surface. The Met describes the process in its essay on the Chinese tradition: the enclosures, called cloisons, are filled with enamel colored by metallic oxide, the piece is fired at roughly 800°C, and because the enamel shrinks after firing, the filling and firing steps are repeated several times before the surface is polished smooth and the exposed wire edges gilded.

An earliest surviving example cannot be identified from the references used here. The pictured Byzantine box belongs to the beginning of the ninth century: the Met places it around AD 800, while other accounts propose 815 or 843. Egyptian and Mycenaean goldwork have earlier enameling histories. A date assigned to this particular reliquary cannot settle the age of every related technique.

In cloisonné, the enamel-holding cells, or cloisons, are built up by soldering or pasting metal wire onto the object's surface. In champlevé, the cells are carved, etched, or cast directly into the metal itself, per Wikipedia's explanation of the two methods. Champlevé's cells can be cut into cheaper copper or bronze, while cloisonné traditionally required wire made of gold or silver, a cost difference that helped champlevé spread faster across medieval Western Europe.

Copper and bronze made champlevé less expensive than construction with precious-metal wire. The Wikipedia account links its expansion to Romanesque art and describes Limoges as a major centre around the 1150s, exporting decorated reliquary boxes across Europe. Byzantine workshops still made cloisonné. Lower material costs help explain the European shift, without proving that cost alone determined every workshop's choice.
